newsitem.title: CHINA: Gore arrives in China to discuss rights, donations.
newsitem.headline: Gore arrives in China to discuss rights, donations.

text.p: U.S. Vice President Al Gore arrived in Beijing on Monday for talks that will mix U.S. desires for better relations with concerns over human rights and a scandal over alleged Chinese political donations.

"I have travelled here to reaffirm the vital importance of relations between our nations, and to continue building a lasting peace between China and the United States," Gore said in an arrival statement.

"The landscape of U.S.-China relations is filled with many rivers, some flowing together, others apart," Gore said at the start of his four-day visit. "Such variety befits the interaction of two great nations and civilisations."

Hoping to end a diplomatic chill that cooled ties for the last two years, Gore stepped off of Air Force Two to become the highest-ranking U.S. official to visit China since President George Bush in 1989 -- just months before Chinese troops crushed pro-democracy protesters in Tiananmen Square.

After talks earlier in the day in Tokyo with Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, Gore said he would raise U.S. concerns about treatment of dissidents in China in talks with Chinese officials. He is to meet Premier Li Peng on Tuesday and President Jiang Zemin on Wednesday.

"I will of course discuss human rights with the leadership of China," Gore said. "Nor will it be a surprise to them to have these matters raised...These issues are important to us as Americans because of who we are."

Although Gore has no plans to meet privately with dissidents, officials travelling with him said some Chinese "critics" of government policy have been invited to a Wednesday night dinner at the U.S. embassy.
A sister of China's most prominent dissident, veteran democracy activist Wei Jingsheng, has appealed to Gore to ask Chinese leaders to free him from a 14-year jail term.
In its annual report on human rights, the U.S. State Department accused Beijing of effectively silencing public dissent in 1996 through jailings, intimidation or exile.

One of the subjects Gore may prefer not to raise but may be unable to avoid involves an FBI investigation into allegations that China illegally tried to funnel contributions into U.S. President Bill Clinton's re-election campaign.

China has denied the allegations, and the official People's Daily said on Monday Beijing had not made any payments to the Democratic Party and that an improvement in Sino-U.S. ties was due to efforts by the two governments and their peoples.

The controversy over U.S. accusations that China may have made illegal contributions to the Democratic Party cast a cloud over the four-day visit aimed at healing ties damaged by disputes ranging from human rights to trade and Taiwan.
But responding to the political uproar at home, Gore has said he would raise the issue in official talks.

U.S. officials said trade issues such as Beijing's growing trade surplus with the United States, its bid to join the World Trade Organisation and renewal of its favourable trading status with Washington would be discussed.
Also on the table will be environmental issues and the future of Hong Kong, which reverts to Beijing sovereignty after 150 years of British colonial rule on July 1.

"The great powers must work together in building new structures of cooperation and communication both within and among nations," Gore said, citing the poem "On Stork Tower" by Tang dynasty (618-907) poet Wang Zhi-huan.

"To see the currents of greatest confluence, we must continue climbing the steps of Stork Tower," Gore said. "That is why I am here. And that is why our two presidents will themselves ascend the tower in the coming months."
Jiang is expected to make a state visit to Washington later this year and U.S. President Bill Clinton plans to come to China in 1998.
